questions.question: List four applications of TEM.
questions.solution_html:
• List four applications of TEM.
  • a) TEM provides detailed images of atomic arrangements and crystal structures in materials.
  • b) It is used to study nanomaterials such as nanoparticles and nanowires to understand their size and internal structure.
  • c) In biology and medicine, TEM reveals detailed views of cells, viruses, and bacteria to study diseases and cell functions.
  • d) It helps analyze and improve metals, alloys, and other materials for advanced industrial and electronic applications.
  • (Any four applications of TEM – (4 marks))

  • preparation.

questions.question: Describe how magnetic nanoparticles help in enviornmental / remediation.
questions.solution_html:
• Magnetic nanoparticles play a key role in environmental remediation due to their large surface area, reactivity, and easy magnetic
  • separation. They can adsorb or degrade pollutants such as heavy metals, dyes, and organic contaminants from water and soil.
  • Functionalized magnetic nanoparticles can be tailored with specific coatings to selectively capture target pollutants. After treatment
  • they can be easily removed from the environment using an external magnetic field, minimizing secondary pollution. Iron oxide
  • nanoparticles, for example, are widely used to remove arsenic, lead, and chromium from contaminated water. Their reusability and
  • high efficiency make them a sustainable and cost-effective tool for cleaning up environmental pollutants.
  • (Any valid 5 points - (7 marks))

questions.question: Discuss the advantages of nanotechnology-based diagnosis over / conventional methods.
questions.solution_html:
• Nanotechnology-based diagnostic methods offer several advantages over conventional approaches. They provide high sensitivity
  • and specificity, allowing detection of minute quantities of biomolecules and enabling early disease diagnosis. The tests are rapid and
  • efficient, significantly reducing the time required for obtaining results. Owing to miniaturization, nanodiagnostic devices are portable
  • and suitable for point-of-care testing. They also allow simultaneous detection of multiple biomarkers, giving a more comprehensive
  • understanding of disease states. Many of these techniques are non-invasive, using samples such as saliva or urine instead of tissue
  • biopsies. Nanoparticles enhance signal generation, leading to greater accuracy and reliability. These systems can also be integrated
  • with digital and smartphone-based platforms for real-time monitoring. Furthermore, they require smaller sample volumes, making
  • them cost-effective, and support personalized medicine by enabling precise biomarker identification for individualized treatment
  • strategies.
  • ( Any valid 5 points - (7 marks))

questions.question: Discuss the principle of AFM. Evaluate its importance in the / characterization of nanomaterials. Discuss Richard Feynman’s hypothesis on atomic-scale manipulation
questions.solution_html:
• The principle of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) is based on scanning a sharp tip on a flexible cantilever over a surface and
  • detecting the intermolecular forces between the tip and the sample. As the tip scans, it experiences forces (attractive or repulsive)
  • that cause the cantilever to bend or change its oscillation. This deflection is detected by a laser beam that reflects off the back of the
  • cantilever onto a position-sensitive photodiode, which translates the movement into a 3D image of the sample's surface topography.
  • AFM can image surfaces at the nanometer and even atomic scale, offering exceptional detail. Unlike many microscopes, AFM
  • provides true 3D topographical maps of the sample surface. AFM can operate in air, vacuum, or liquid, making it suitable for both
  • biological and material samples.
  • (Principle of AFM- (4 marks); Importance of AFM - any 3 points - (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: (Principle of AFM- ; Importance of AFM - any 3 points - )

  • could make even smaller machines, like today’s nanorobots. He talked about storing large amounts of information in very small
  • space. His ideas inspired modern fields such as nanoscience, nanomedicine, and microelectronics. Feynman’s vision came true

questions.question: Explain the importance of UV - Visible spectra and IR spectra in the / characterization of nanomaterials
questions.solution_html:
• UV-Vis spectroscopy helps find the size and concentration of nanomaterials by measuring light absorption. Nanoparticles like gold
  • and silver show a special feature called surface plasmon resonance (SPR), where free electrons resonate with electromagnetic
  • radiation, causing strong absorption peaks. SPR peaks in UV-Visible spectra reveal the size, shape, and stability of nanoparticles in
  • solution.
  • IR spectroscopy identifies the chemical bonds and groups on nanomaterial surfaces. It helps confirm if the nanomaterial contains
  • specific molecules or coating substances. IR gives information about how atoms in nanomaterials are bonded and changes during
  • reactions
  • (Relevant explanation, UV – (3.5 marks), IR – (3.5 marks))

questions.question: Describe different types of nanomaterials based on their dimensionality.
questions.solution_html:
• Zero-dimensional (0D): All three dimensions are in the nanoscale (1–100 nm). Examples: nanoparticles, quantum
  • dots, fullerenes, dendrimers.
  • One-dimensional (1D): Two dimensions are in the nanoscale and one dimension is >100 nm. Examples: carbon
  • nanotubes, nanowires, nanorods, nanofibres.
  • Two-dimensional (2D): One dimension is in the nanoscale and two dimensions are >100 nm. Examples: graphene
  • graphyne, borophene, phosphorene, nanofilms and nanocoatings.
  • Three-dimensional (3D): All three dimensions are >100 nm, but the material is composed of nanoscale building
  • blocks or possesses nanoscale features. Examples: nanocomposites, nanoparticle dispersions, bundles of
  • nanotubes/nanowires.
  • (Relevant explanation - (4 marks))

  • bonding of nanomaterials.
  • Applications: It is widely used for surface characterization, thin-film analysis, nanomaterial quality control, and

questions.question: Explain the top down approaches used in nanochemistry. Discuss its methods, / principle, advantages and limitations with suitable examples.
questions.solution_html:
• limitations with suitable examples.
  •  Definition & Principle: Top-down approach is the fabrication of nanomaterials by reducing bulk
  • materials into nanosized particles using physical or mechanical methods.
  •  Methods
  •  Ball milling: Bulk material is mechanically ground into nanoparticles using high-energy ball
  • mills.
  •  Lithography: Nanostructures are fabricated by selectively removing or patterning material using
  • light or electron beams.
  •  Laser ablation: A high-energy laser beam vaporizes a solid target to produce nanoparticles.
  •  Advantages: Simple and scalable process; suitable for large-scale production; widely applicable to
  • different materials.
  •  Limitations: Possibility of contamination and poor control over particle size and shape; defects may be
  • introduced during processing.
  •  Examples: Nanoparticles prepared by ball milling, semiconductor nanostructures fabricated by
  • photolithography/electron-beam lithography, and metal nanoparticles produced by laser ablation.
  • (Definition/principle-(2 marks), Any two different methods-(8 marks), advantages -(2 marks), limitation

questions.question: Discuss the advantages of nanotechnology-based diagnosis over / conventional methods.

questions.question: Discuss the principle of AFM. Evaluate its importance in the / characterization of nanomaterials. Discuss Richard Feynman’s hypothesis on atomic-scale manipulation
questions.solution_html:
• The principle of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) is based on scanning a sharp tip on a flexible cantilever over a surface and
  • detecting the intermolecular forces between the tip and the sample. As the tip scans, it experiences forces (attractive or repulsive)
  • that cause the cantilever to bend or change its oscillation. This deflection is detected by a laser beam that reflects off the back of the
  • cantilever onto a position-sensitive photodiode, which translates the movement into a 3D image of the sample's surface topography.
  • AFM can image surfaces at the nanometer and even atomic scale, offering exceptional detail. Unlike many microscopes, AFM
  • provides true 3D topographical maps of the sample surface. AFM can operate in air, vacuum, or liquid, making it suitable for both
  • biological and material samples.
  • (Principle of AFM- (4 marks); Importance of AFM - any 3 points - (3 marks))

  • and silver show a special feature called surface plasmon resonance (SPR), where free electrons resonate with electromagnetic
  • radiation, causing strong absorption peaks. SPR peaks in UV-Visible spectra reveal the size, shape, and stability of nanoparticles in
  • solution.
  • IR spectroscopy identifies the chemical bonds and groups on nanomaterial surfaces. It helps confirm if the nanomaterial contains
  • specific molecules or coating substances. IR gives information about how atoms in nanomaterials are bonded and changes during
  • reactions

  • dots, fullerenes, dendrimers.

  • nanotubes, nanowires, nanorods, nanofibres.
  • Two-dimensional (2D): One dimension is in the nanoscale and two dimensions are >100 nm. Examples: graphene
  • graphyne, borophene, phosphorene, nanofilms and nanocoatings.
  • Three-dimensional (3D): All three dimensions are >100 nm, but the material is composed of nanoscale building
  • blocks or possesses nanoscale features. Examples: nanocomposites, nanoparticle dispersions, bundles of
  • nanotubes/nanowires.

  •  Definition & Principle: Top-down approach is the fabrication of nanomaterials by reducing bulk
  • materials into nanosized particles using physical or mechanical methods.
  •  Methods
  •  Ball milling: Bulk material is mechanically ground into nanoparticles using high-energy ball
  • mills.
  •  Lithography: Nanostructures are fabricated by selectively removing or patterning material using
  • light or electron beams.
  •  Laser ablation: A high-energy laser beam vaporizes a solid target to produce nanoparticles.
  •  Advantages: Simple and scalable process; suitable for large-scale production; widely applicable to
  • different materials.
  •  Limitations: Possibility of contamination and poor control over particle size and shape; defects may be
  • introduced during processing.
  •  Examples: Nanoparticles prepared by ball milling, semiconductor nanostructures fabricated by
  • photolithography/electron-beam lithography, and metal nanoparticles produced by laser ablation.
